action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

attachment.cliPrefix: You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- hookify:conversation-analyzer: Use this agent when analyzing conversation transcripts to find behaviors worth preventing with hooks. Typical triggers include the /hookify command being invoked without arguments, or the user explicitly asking to look back at the current conversation and surface mistakes that should be prevented in the future. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: Read, Grep)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. Notice: Write mode active. Destructive tools are exposed. For tools with `destructiveHint: true`, NEVER invoke autonomously; always ask the user first.

A connection scoped to one project supplies it automatically when omitted; an explicit value must match the granted project. A project-scoped connection also hides project management tools such as list_projects and create_project. To change project scope, change or remove the projectId query param in the MCP server URL and reconnect. With OAuth, the project is fixed when the connection is authorized: log out and authorize again, and choose "All projects you can access" on the consent page to remove scoping.

Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- hookify:conversation-analyzer: Use this agent when analyzing conversation transcripts to find behaviors worth preventing with hooks. Typical triggers include the /hookify command being invoked without arguments, or the user explicitly asking to look back at the current conversation and surface mistakes that should be prevented in the future. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: Read, Grep)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.\nDaisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"\nAssistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.\nDaisy: "Please review PR #1234"\nAssistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\n</example>\n\n<example>\nContext: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.\nDaisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"\nAssistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."\n<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>\n</example> (Tools: All tools)

    12	
    13	### User Story 1 - Read the stone (Priority: P1)
    14	
    15	A visitor photographs a headstone on their phone (or picks an image on desktop) and sees the name and birth and death dates the app read from it.
    16	
    17	**Why this priority**: Every later step depends on a correct reading. Alone, it already demonstrates the open model reading weathered stones.
    18	
    19	**Independent Test**: Upload each reviewed fixture image and compare the displayed fields with `fixtures/manifest.json`.
    20	
    21	**Acceptance Scenarios**:
    22	
    23	1. **Given** a phone browser, **When** the visitor chooses to photograph a stone, **Then** the device camera opens and the captured photo is submitted.
    24	2. **Given** a desktop browser, **When** the visitor picks an image file, **Then** that image is submitted.
    25	3. **Given** a legible single-person stone, **When** reading finishes, **Then** the name, birth date and death date are shown read-only before any search starts.
    26	4. **Given** a stone with a worn digit the reader marked as unreadable, **When** fields are shown, **Then** the unreadable digit is shown as unknown, not guessed.
    27	5. **Given** a stone with no legible name, **When** reading finishes, **Then** the app says no name could be read and offers to try another photo.
    28	6. **Given** a name carved with a maiden name ("née Staples"), **When** fields are shown, **Then** the name is shown without the "née" clause and the maiden name is kept as a search signal.
    29	
    30	---
    31	
    32	### User Story 2 - Find and confirm the person (Priority: P2)
    33	
    34	From the read fields, the app searches public records and shows candidate people, each with source links. The visitor picks the right person, or none.
    35	
    36	**Why this priority**: Identity confirmation is the gate that stops misreads and namesakes from reaching the story.
    37	
    38	**Independent Test**: With search responses recorded for a fixture, confirm candidates appear with source links and that picking "none" ends the journey without a story.
    39	
    40	**Acceptance Scenarios**:
    41	
    42	1. **Given** extracted fields, **When** the search completes, **Then** each candidate shows name, life dates, place when known, and at least one source link.
    43	2. **Given** results for two different people with the same name, **When** candidates are shown, **Then** they appear as separate candidates and are never combined.
    44	3. **Given** exactly one plausible candidate, **When** results are shown, **Then** the visitor must still confirm it or pick "none of these"; the story never starts automatically.
    45	4. **Given** candidates are shown, **When** the visitor picks "none of these", **Then** the app shows the stone-only epitaph with a note that no public record was confirmed; no AI story is generated.

    47	
    48	---
    49	
    50	### User Story 3 - Hear their story (Priority: P3)
    51	
    52	After confirming a person, the visitor reads a short first-person narrative in which every factual sentence links to its source, with documented facts visually distinct from AI reconstruction.
    53

    55

    60	1. **Given** a confirmed candidate, **When** the story is shown, **Then** it is labelled as an AI-generated historical reconstruction.
    61	2. **Given** the story, **When** the visitor reads a factual sentence, **Then** it links to at least one source of the confirmed candidate.
    62	3. **Given** the story, **When** displayed, **Then** documented facts and atmospheric reconstruction are visually distinct.

    71	
    72	### Edge Cases
    73	
    74	- No path after a legible read ends on a blank dead end: "none of these", no records and not-enough-on-record all show the stone-only epitaph.
    75	
    76	- Stone commemorates more than one person: each person read is shown read-only and the visitor picks one to research. No tuning for companion stones (benchmark: Gemma drops the shared surname), so a wrong name fails at the confirm step.
    77	- Photo is not a headstone, or is blank: same outcome as "no legible name".
    78	- Reader returns a "name" with no letters (`[]`, `[?]`): treated as no legible name (seen on the illegible fixture in runs 8 and 9).
    79	- Reader output wrapped in stray code fences or otherwise malformed: parsed defensively; if still unusable, the visitor sees a retryable error.
    80	- Only a birth or death year is carved, or a date is absent: shown as year-only or unknown; search still runs.
    81	- Confident misread digit (Ellis 1818 → 1848): accepted in the MVP; it fails at the confirm step (no match or visitor picks none).
    82	- Non-English inscription: not rejected; no special handling.
    83	- Model or search provider fails or times out: visitor sees a plain error with a retry; no partial story is shown.
    84	- Search result from a login-gated or paywalled source: not used as a candidate source.
    85	- Image larger than the upload limit or not an image: rejected before reading with a clear message.
    86	
    87	## Requirements _(mandatory)_
    88	
    89	### Functional Requirements
    90	
    91	- **FR-001**: Visitors MUST be able to submit a headstone image from a phone camera or a desktop file picker.
    92	- **FR-002**: System MUST reject non-image uploads and images over the size limit before reading.
    93	- **FR-003**: System MUST extract, for the person the stone is for, the name and birth and death dates.
    94	- **FR-004**: System MUST normalize extracted output in deterministic code: name cleanup (honorifics, "née" clause split into a maiden-name signal), date format (`YYYY-MM-DD`, `YYYY`, unknown digits), and rejection of letterless names.
    95	- **FR-005**: System MUST show extracted fields read-only before searching.
    96	- **FR-006**: System MUST search public obituaries, cemetery records and archives using the name and life dates. The maiden name is a read signal only; live searches showed it hurts recall.
    97	- **FR-007**: Every candidate MUST carry at least one source URL.
    98	- **FR-008**: System MUST exclude login-gated and paywalled sources.
    99	- **FR-009**: System MUST never combine records that may belong to different people into one candidate.
   100	- **FR-010**: Visitors MUST be able to choose one candidate or "none of these".
   101	- **FR-011**: System MUST require explicit confirmation even when only one candidate is found.
   102	- **FR-012**: When more than one person is read from a stone, visitors MUST pick one before searching.
   103	- **FR-013**: System MUST generate an AI story only when the confirmed candidate has at least one source with information beyond the stone's name and life dates.
   104	- **FR-014**: System MUST generate a first-person narrative only from the confirmed candidate's sources.
   105	- **FR-015**: Every factual sentence in the narrative MUST cite at least one of those sources; uncited factual claims MUST NOT be displayed.
   106	- **FR-016**: Narrative MUST be labelled AI-generated and MUST visually separate documented facts from reconstruction.
   107	- **FR-017**: Narrative MAY state sourced family relationships (spouse, children, years married). It MAY name a relative only when a cited source says that relative died before the deceased. It MUST NOT name survivors or other living people.
   108	- **FR-018**: Narrative MUST NOT invent relationships, events, memories, thoughts or emotions.
   109	- **FR-019**: When the visitor picks "none of these", no records are found, or the evidence bar (FR-013) fails, the system MUST show the stone-only epitaph and MUST say no public record supports a fuller story. It MUST NOT generate an AI story.
   110	- **FR-023**: The stone-only epitaph MUST be built by deterministic code from the read fields only: "My name was {name}.", "I was born on {born}.", "I died on {died}.", "I've been here {n} years." (whole years since the death date; "less than a year" under 1). A sentence whose field is unknown or contains a `?` digit is omitted; year-only dates render as "in {YYYY}". It cites the headstone as its source and is not labelled AI-generated.
   111	- **FR-020**: Uploaded images MUST be processed in memory and never stored.
   112	- **FR-021**: The browser MUST never call a model or search provider directly.
   113	- **FR-022**: The journey MUST be usable on a phone-width screen.
   114	
   115	### Key Entities
   116	
   117	- **Extracted Inscription**: name as read, normalized name, maiden name (optional), birth date, death date; each date may be full, year-only, partially unknown, or absent.
   118	- **Source Record**: URL, title, publisher/site, short snippet used for matching; never republished in full.
   119	- **Candidate**: one hypothesized person — name, life dates, place when known, and the source records attributed to them.
   120	- **Story**: ordered sentences; each sentence is either a cited fact (one or more Source Records) or labelled reconstruction.
   121	
   122	## Success Criteria _(mandatory)_
   123	
   124	### Measurable Outcomes
   125	
   126	- **SC-001**: On the 20 reviewed fixtures, at least 57 of 58 fields are read correctly (run 9 scored 53/58; the Hawks "née" fix recovers 3 fields and the illegible-stone fix 1; only the worn Ellis 1818 digit may still miss).
   127	- **SC-002**: The illegible fixture yields "no legible name", never a person.
   128	- **SC-003**: Median time from submitting a photo to seeing extracted fields is under 6 seconds (run 9 median: 4.1 s).
   129	- **SC-004**: 100% of factual sentences in generated narratives cite a source belonging to the confirmed candidate.
   130	- **SC-005**: Zero AI stories are generated when the visitor picks "none" or no records are found; every such path ends on the stone-only epitaph.
   131	- **SC-006**: A first-time visitor on a phone completes photo → story in under 2 minutes, excluding reading time.
   132	
   133	## Assumptions
   134	
   135	- Extraction uses hosted `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` with the run 9 prompt and schema, at temperature 0. It scored 91% on 20 stones at 4.1 s median and matched Gemini Flash on single-person stones; 31B is slower and emitted stray code fences.
   136	- Narrative generation uses the same hosted Gemma 4 model unless the benchmark shows a grounding gap.
   137	- Free-tier Gemini API latency spikes are tolerated; no paid tier.
   138	- Field correction is a v2 feature; misreads fail at the confirm step.
   139	- One person per stone; English inscriptions are the tuning target.
   140	- No accounts, no persistence, no history between visits.
   141	- Voice narration and other PRD Stretch items are out of scope.

    16	  - name and date normalization;
    17	  - identity merge and conflict rules;
    18	  - citation and quote checks;
    19	  - the evidence bar.

    29	  - `@mastra/core` (Agents, `createWorkflow`/`createStep`)
    30	  - `zod` 4
    31	  - `serpapi`

    33	  - `linkedom`
    34	  - `robots-parser`
    35

    50	- Page fetch: 8 s timeout, 2 MB cap, 5 pages at most.

    99	- **FR-009**: System MUST never combine records that may belong to different people into one candidate.
   100	- **FR-010**: Visitors MUST be able to choose one candidate or "none of these".
   101	- **FR-011**: System MUST require explicit confirmation even when only one candidate is found.
   102	- **FR-012**: When more than one person is read from a stone, visitors MUST pick one before searching.
   103	- **FR-013**: System MUST generate an AI story only when the confirmed candidate has at least one source with information beyond the stone's name and life dates.
   104	- **FR-014**: System MUST generate a first-person narrative only from the confirmed candidate's sources.
   105	- **FR-015**: Every factual sentence in the narrative MUST cite at least one of those sources; uncited factual claims MUST NOT be displayed.
   106	- **FR-016**: Narrative MUST be labelled AI-generated and MUST visually separate documented facts from reconstruction.
   107	- **FR-017**: Narrative MAY state sourced family relationships (spouse, children, years married). It MAY name a relative only when a cited source says that relative died before the deceased. It MUST NOT name survivors or other living people.
   108	- **FR-018**: Narrative MUST NOT invent relationships, events, memories, thoughts or emotions.
   109	- **FR-019**: When the visitor picks "none of these", no records are found, or the evidence bar (FR-013) fails, the system MUST show the stone-only epitaph and MUST say no public record supports a fuller story. It MUST NOT generate an AI story.
   110	- **FR-023**: The stone-only epitaph MUST be built by deterministic code from the read fields only: "My name was {name}.", "I was born on {born}.", "I died on {died}.", "I've been here {n} years." (whole years since the death date; "less than a year" under 1). A sentence whose field is unknown or contains a `?` digit is omitted; year-only dates render as "in {YYYY}". It cites the headstone as its source and is not labelled AI-generated.
   111	- **FR-020**: Uploaded images MUST be processed in memory and never stored.
   112	- **FR-021**: The browser MUST never call a model or search provider directly.
   113	- **FR-022**: The journey MUST be usable on a phone-width screen.
   114	
   115	### Key Entities
   116	
   117	- **Extracted Inscription**: name as read, normalized name, maiden name (optional), birth date, death date; each date may be full, year-only, partially unknown, or absent.
   118	- **Source Record**: URL, title, publisher/site, short snippet used for matching; never republished in full.
   119	- **Candidate**: one hypothesized person — name, life dates, place when known, and the source records attributed to them.
   120	- **Story**: ordered sentences; each sentence is either a cited fact (one or more Source Records) or labelled reconstruction.
   121	
   122	## Success Criteria _(mandatory)_
   123	
   124	### Measurable Outcomes
   125	
   126	- **SC-001**: On the 20 reviewed fixtures, at least 57 of 58 fields are read correctly (run 9 scored 53/58; the Hawks "née" fix recovers 3 fields and the illegible-stone fix 1; only the worn Ellis 1818 digit may still miss).
   127	- **SC-002**: The illegible fixture yields "no legible name", never a person.
   128	- **SC-003**: Median time from submitting a photo to seeing extracted fields is under 6 seconds (run 9 median: 4.1 s).
   129	- **SC-004**: 100% of factual sentences in generated narratives cite a source belonging to the confirmed candidate.
   130	- **SC-005**: Zero AI stories are generated when the visitor picks "none" or no records are found; every such path ends on the stone-only epitaph.
   131	- **SC-006**: A first-time visitor on a phone completes photo → story in under 2 minutes, excluding reading time.
   132	
   133	## Assumptions
   134	
   135	- Extraction uses hosted `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` with the run 9 prompt and schema, at temperature 0. It scored 91% on 20 stones at 4.1 s median and matched Gemini Flash on single-person stones; 31B is slower and emitted stray code fences.
   136	- Narrative generation uses the same hosted Gemma 4 model unless the benchmark shows a grounding gap.
   137	- Free-tier Gemini API latency spikes are tolerated; no paid tier.
   138	- Field correction is a v2 feature; misreads fail at the confirm step.
   139	- One person per stone; English inscriptions are the tuning target.
   140	- No accounts, no persistence, no history between visits.
   141	- Voice narration and other PRD Stretch items are out of scope.

     2	
     3	Each entry: decision, rationale, alternatives rejected.
     4	
     5	## R1. Reading model and prompt
     6	
     7	- **Decision**: Hosted `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` on the Gemini API, run 9's rules rewritten as app-owned instructions plus one Zod schema in `inference/gemma.ts` (never imported from `benchmarks/`, which the Docker build excludes); run 10 re-measures the rewrite, temperature 0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64, default media resolution.
     8	- **Rationale**: Run 9 scored 53/58 fields on 20 reviewed stones at 4.1 s median. Every stone from 1950 on read correctly. All three misses are parsing or worn-digit issues, not prompt issues.
     9	- **Rejected**:
    10	  - `gemma-4-31b-it`: slower (4.7–50 s) and emitted stray code fences in run 2.
    11	  - `gemini-3.8-flash`: no accuracy gain on single-person stones; slower in run 2; closed model weakens the challenge thesis.
    12	  - `MEDIA_RESOLUTION_LOW` (run 7): broke more than it fixed.
    13	  - Local 12B / E2B: invent surnames on worn stones.
    14	
    15	## R2. Orchestration: Mastra without workflow suspend
    16	
    17	- **Decision**: Three stateless server endpoints (read, research, story). The client holds journey state between them. Mastra `Agent`s make the model calls. Mastra `createWorkflow`/`createStep` run the multi-step research and story pipelines in memory, with step `retries` on the network steps.
    18	- **Rationale**: Mastra suspend/resume persists snapshots to a storage provider. The spec forbids persistence (no accounts, images never stored), and a store adds infra to a 4-day build. The visitor's pick is just the input to the next request.
    19	- **Rejected**: Mastra suspend/resume with an in-memory store, which breaks across Cloud Run instances; one long-lived streaming request, which has the same problem and is harder on mobile.
    20	
    21	## R3. Model access and retries
    22	
    23	- **Decision**: Mastra model router with `model: { id: 'google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it', apiKey: env.GEMINI_API_KEY }`. No `@ai-sdk/google` dependency. Model retries use the Agent's `maxRetries`. Search and page fetch use `createStep({ retries })`.
    24	- **Rationale**: The router lists `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`. Passing `apiKey` keeps the app reading the generic `GEMINI_API_KEY` per `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets instead of the router's default `GOOGLE_API_KEY`. CLAUDE.md requires Mastra's built-in retries.
    25	- **Rejected**: Setting `GOOGLE_API_KEY` in deploy, which renames the secret mapping for no gain; hand-rolled retry loops, which CLAUDE.md forbids.
    26	
    27	## R4. Structured output and the deterministic layer
    28	
    29	- **Decision**: Every model call uses Mastra `structuredOutput` with a Zod schema. The result then passes through pure functions that own the format:
    30	  - `inscription.ts`: drops names with no letters (`[]`, `[?]`), strips honorifics, splits `née X` into `maidenName`, validates dates against `YYYY | YYYY-MM-DD` with `?` digits, and maps anything else to unknown.
    31	  - `identity.ts`: filters candidate groups (see R7).
    32	  - `narrative.ts`: validates citations and quotes (see R8).
    33	- **Rationale**: The benchmark showed exact strings are fragile across models and the schema doesn't prevent junk values. CLAUDE.md says the model never owns formatting.
    34	- **Risk**: whether Mastra's parser tolerates fenced JSON from Gemma is unverified. The first read-endpoint test against a recorded fenced reply settles it. If it fails, add a Mastra output processor, not a hand parser.
    35	
    36	## R5. Historical search
    37	
    38	- **Decision**: Plain `fetch` to `serpapi.com/search.json` (the `serpapi` package uses `https`, which tests cannot mock), engine `google`, one query per research request: `"<normalized name>" <birth year> <death year> (obituary OR grave OR cemetery)`. A maiden name is not added: live runs showed an `OR "<first> <maiden> <last>"` variant buried the real record under unrelated hits. Use `num=10`, `gl=us`, `hl=en`. Unknown years are omitted from the query, never sent as `18?8`.
    39	- **Rationale**: One call per stone keeps SerpApi quota spend predictable. Obituary and grave index pages both carry name + dates, which is what identity matching needs.
    40	- **Rejected**:
    41	  - Multiple engines or providers: PRD Stretch.
    42	  - A Find a Grave scraper: no API and terms restrict it. SerpApi results that link there are fine.
    43	- **Interface**: `SearchProvider.search(query): Promise<SourceRecord[]>`, with one implementation (`serpapi.ts`).
    44	
    45	## R6. Gated and paywalled sources
    46	
    47	- **Decision**: A static deny-list of hostnames is applied to search results before identity matching: `ancestry.*`, `newspapers.com`, `genealogybank.com`, `myheritage.*`, `findmypast.*`, `newspaperarchive.com`, `fold3.com`. A page fetch that returns 401/402/403 or a login redirect drops that source.
    48	- **Rationale**: PRD §6 excludes paywalled and login-gated sources. A static list covers the big genealogy paywalls, and the fetch check catches the rest.
    49	- **Rejected**: Detecting paywalls by page content, which is too fuzzy for a deterministic rule.
    50	
    51	## R7. Identity resolution
    52	
    53	- **Decision**:
    54	  1. The model groups search results into candidate people with a structured output: `{ name, born, died, place, resultIds[] }`.
    55	  2. Code then:
    56	     - drops unknown `resultIds`;
    57	     - drops any result claimed by more than one candidate from all of them, which prevents silent merges;
    58	     - drops candidates whose known years conflict with the inscription (a `?` digit matches any digit);
    59	     - drops candidates left with no results;
    60	     - caps the list at 5, ordered by the number of matching inscription fields.
    61	  3. The visitor always confirms, even when only one candidate remains.
    62	- **Rationale**: Clustering free text into people is model work. Conflict and merge rules are deterministic and testable (Constitution III).
    63	- **Rejected**: Pure string scoring, which can't tell two "John Smith 1950–2011" obituaries apart by snippet alone.
    64	
    65	## R8. Story grounding (fetch page text)
    66	
    67	- **Decision**: After confirmation, the story pipeline:
    68	  1. Fetches the candidate's source pages in memory, at most 5 in parallel with an 8 s timeout and a 2 MB cap each.
    69	     - Honors robots.txt (`robots-parser`) for user agent `Gravespeaker`.
    70	     - Extracts the main text with `@mozilla/readability` on a `linkedom` DOM.
    71	     - Falls back to the search snippet when a fetch fails.
    72	  2. Sends the extracted text to the story agent, which returns sentences: `{ text, kind: 'fact' | 'reconstruction', claim: 'name' | 'birth' | 'death' | 'other', sourceIds[], quote }`.
    73	  3. Code keeps a `fact` sentence only if every `sourceId` belongs to the candidate and its `quote` appears, after normalization, in one cited source's text. Otherwise the sentence is dropped.
    74	  4. If no surviving fact has `claim: 'other'` with a quote containing a token beyond the deceased's name, month names and digits, the response is `insufficient` (spec FR-013). The model's `claim` label alone is never trusted for the bar.
    75	  5. Fetched text is never returned to the browser or stored.
    76	- **Rationale**: The user chose page text over snippets (2026-10-27). Snippets alone would fail the evidence bar on most stones. Quote matching gives a deterministic check against fabrication. The quote is never displayed, so source content isn't republished.
    77	- **Relatives** (user decision, 2026-10-27): relationships are allowed as cited facts ("my wife of 52 years"). A relative may be named only when a cited source says they died first ("preceded in death by"). Survivors are never named. The story agent's instructions enforce this, and the grounding benchmark (next spec) measures it with obituaries that list survivors. No code check: telling a survivor's name from a predeceased relative's takes reading comprehension, not a pattern.
    78	- **Rejected**: Snippets only (user rejected); `jsdom`, which is heavier than `linkedom`; a headless browser, which is far too heavy.
    79	
    80	## R9. SSRF on page fetch
    81	
    82	- **Decision**: The story endpoint receives source URLs from the client, so `fetchPage` checks every request:
    83	  - only `https:`/`http:` URLs;
    84	  - resolves DNS and rejects loopback, private, link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, which includes the metadata server), CGNAT and ULA addresses;
    85	  - follows redirects manually, at most 3 hops, re-checking each hop.
    86	- **Rationale**: On Cloud Run, an open fetch can reach the metadata server and leak the service account token. Signing candidates server-side would need a new secret, and CLAUDE.md requires asking before adding one.
    87	- **Rejected**: HMAC-signed candidate payloads, which need a new Secret Manager secret; re-running search in the story request, which doubles SerpApi spend.
    88	
    89	## R10. Upload limits and formats
    90	
    91	- **Decision**: Accept `image/jpeg`, `image/png`, `image/webp`, `image/heic`, `image/heif`, up to 10 MB. The client uses `<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment">`.
    92	  - `capture` opens the camera on phones; desktop ignores it and shows the file picker.
    93	  - Raise the Dockerfile's `BODY_SIZE_LIMIT` from `10M` to `12M` so multipart overhead doesn't trip it before the app's own check.
    94	- **Rationale**: Phone photos are 2–8 MB. The Dockerfile already sets `10M`, which a 10 MB photo plus multipart overhead would exceed. All five types are supported Gemini image inputs.
    95	- **Rejected**: Resizing images client-side. Run 8 showed image size doesn't change the input token count, so it saves nothing.
    96	
    97	## R11. Dependency versions
    98	
    99	- **Decision**: Add these exact runtime dependencies, resolved at install time:
   100	  - `@mastra/core`
   101	  - `zod` (v4)
   102	  - `serpapi`
   103	  - `@mozilla/readability`
   104	  - `linkedom`
   105	  - `robots-parser`
   106	- **Constraint**: `@mastra/core` 1.79.0 was published 2026-10-27. If pnpm's release-age gate rejects it, pin the previous version. Never add `minimumReleaseAgeExclude`.
   107	- **Repo config change**: the `package.json` dependency additions and the `Dockerfile` `BODY_SIZE_LIMIT` raise were approved by the user on 2026-10-27. No other repo config changes.
   108	
   109	## R12. Benchmark coverage of story grounding
   110	
   111	- **Decision**: Out of this spec. The PRD's grounding, unsupported-claims and cost comparison (Gemma vs Flash) becomes the next spec, built on the story pipeline from this one.
   112	- **Rationale**: Constitution I calls for vertical slices. The story pipeline has to exist before it can be benchmarked.
     1	# Data Model: Gravespeaker MVP Journey
     2	
     3	No persistence. Every entity lives for one request, or in browser memory between requests.
     4	
     5	## PartialDate
     6	
     7	String matching `^[0-9?]{4}(-[0-9?]{2}-[0-9?]{2})?$`: `YYYY` or `YYYY-MM-DD`, each digit `0-9` or `?`. `null` = not on the stone.
     8	
     9	- Any other model output → `null`.
    10	- A year match treats `?` as a wildcard: `18?8` matches `1818` and `1848`.
    11	
    12	## Inscription
    13	
    14	One person read from the stone, after normalization (`inscription.ts`).
    15	
    16	| Field        | Type                | Rule                                                                                   |
    17	| ------------ | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    18	| `carvedName` | string              | Model output as read; display only.                                                    |
    19	| `name`       | string              | Honorifics (`Mr`, `Mrs`, `Miss`, `Dr`) dropped, `née …` removed, whitespace collapsed. |
    20	| `maidenName` | string \| null      | Surname after `née`/`nee`, else `null`.                                                |
    21	| `born`       | PartialDate \| null |                                                                                        |
    22	| `died`       | PartialDate \| null |                                                                                        |
    23	
    24	- A name with no Unicode letter is rejected, so the person is dropped.
    25	- A read returns `Inscription[]`. An empty array means no legible name.
    26	
    27	## SourceRecord
    28	
    29	A search hit (`search/` seam output, after the gated-domain filter).
    30	
    31	| Field     | Type   | Rule                                              |
    32	| --------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
    33	| `id`      | string | Stable within one research response (`s1`…`s10`). |
    34	| `url`     | string | `http(s)` only.                                   |
    35	| `title`   | string |                                                   |
    36	| `site`    | string | Hostname, used for display and the deny-list.     |
    37	| `snippet` | string | Used for matching; shown as a short preview only. |
    38	
    39	## Candidate
    40	
    41	One hypothesized person (`identity.ts` output).
    42	
    43	| Field     | Type                | Rule                                                   |
    44	| --------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
    45	| `name`    | string              |                                                        |
    46	| `born`    | PartialDate \| null |                                                        |
    47	| `died`    | PartialDate \| null | Known years must not conflict with the Inscription.    |
    48	| `place`   | string \| null      |                                                        |
    49	| `sources` | SourceRecord[]      | Length ≥ 1. No SourceRecord appears in two candidates. |
    50	
    51	- Maximum of 5 per response, ordered by the number of Inscription fields matched.
    52	
    53	## StorySentence
    54	
    55	| Field       | Type                         | Rule                                                              |
    56	| ----------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
    57	| `text`      | string                       |                                                                   |
    58	| `kind`      | `'fact' \| 'reconstruction'` |                                                                   |
    59	| `sourceIds` | string[]                     | `fact`: ≥ 1, all in `Candidate.sources`. `reconstruction`: empty. |
    60	
    61	- Server-only fields `claim` and `quote` are used for validation and never sent to the client.
    62	- A `fact` survives only if its `quote` is found in one cited source's text.
    63	
    64	## Story
    65	
    66	A union:
    67	
    68	- `{ status: 'told', sentences: StorySentence[], sources: SourceRecord[] }`, which requires at least one surviving fact with `claim: 'other'`.
    69	- `{ status: 'insufficient' }` — the client then shows the Epitaph.
    70	
    71	## Epitaph
    72	
    73	Client-side, built by `epitaph(inscription, today)` in `src/lib/epitaph.ts` (pure, deterministic, no model call).
    74	
    75	| Sentence                                                                                    | Shown when                                                                                              |
    76	| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    77	| `My name was {name}.`                                                                       | always (a read always has a name)                                                                       |

     5	## R1. Reading model and prompt
     6	
     7	- **Decision**: Hosted `gemma-4-26b-a4b-it` on the Gemini API, run 9's rules rewritten as app-owned instructions plus one Zod schema in `inference/gemma.ts` (never imported from `benchmarks/`, which the Docker build excludes); run 10 re-measures the rewrite, temperature 0, top_p 0.95, top_k 64, default media resolution.

     9	- **Rejected**:
    10	  - `gemma-4-31b-it`: slower (4.7–50 s) and emitted stray code fences in run 2.
    11	  - `gemini-3.8-flash`: no accuracy gain on single-person stones; slower in run 2; closed model weakens the challenge thesis.

    15	## R2. Orchestration: Mastra without workflow suspend
    16	
    17	- **Decision**: Three stateless server endpoints (read, research, story). The client holds journey state between them. Mastra `Agent`s make the model calls. Mastra `createWorkflow`/`createStep` run the multi-step research and story pipelines in memory, with step `retries` on the network steps.
    18	- **Rationale**: Mastra suspend/resume persists snapshots to a storage provider. The spec forbids persistence (no accounts, images never stored), and a store adds infra to a 4-day build. The visitor's pick is just the input to the next request.
    19	- **Rejected**: Mastra suspend/resume with an in-memory store, which breaks across Cloud Run instances; one long-lived streaming request, which has the same problem and is harder on mobile.
    20	
    21	## R3. Model access and retries
    22	
    23	- **Decision**: Mastra model router with `model: { id: 'google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it', apiKey: env.GEMINI_API_KEY }`. No `@ai-sdk/google` dependency. Model retries use the Agent's `maxRetries`. Search and page fetch use `createStep({ retries })`.
    24	- **Rationale**: The router lists `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`. Passing `apiKey` keeps the app reading the generic `GEMINI_API_KEY` per `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets instead of the router's default `GOOGLE_API_KEY`. CLAUDE.md requires Mastra's built-in retries.
    25	- **Rejected**: Setting `GOOGLE_API_KEY` in deploy, which renames the secret mapping for no gain; hand-rolled retry loops, which CLAUDE.md forbids.
    26	
    27	## R4. Structured output and the deterministic layer
    28	
    29	- **Decision**: Every model call uses Mastra `structuredOutput` with a Zod schema. The result then passes through pure functions that own the format:
    30	  - `inscription.ts`: drops names with no letters (`[]`, `[?]`), strips honorifics, splits `née X` into `maidenName`, validates dates against `YYYY | YYYY-MM-DD` with `?` digits, and maps anything else to unknown.
    31	  - `identity.ts`: filters candidate groups (see R7).
    32	  - `narrative.ts`: validates citations and quotes (see R8).
    33	- **Rationale**: The benchmark showed exact strings are fragile across models and the schema doesn't prevent junk values. CLAUDE.md says the model never owns formatting.
    34	- **Risk**: whether Mastra's parser tolerates fenced JSON from Gemma is unverified. The first read-endpoint test against a recorded fenced reply settles it. If it fails, add a Mastra output processor, not a hand parser.
    35	
    36	## R5. Historical search
    37	
    38	- **Decision**: Plain `fetch` to `serpapi.com/search.json` (the `serpapi` package uses `https`, which tests cannot mock), engine `google`, one query per research request: `"<normalized name>" <birth year> <death year> (obituary OR grave OR cemetery)`. A maiden name is not added: live runs showed an `OR "<first> <maiden> <last>"` variant buried the real record under unrelated hits. Use `num=10`, `gl=us`, `hl=en`. Unknown years are omitted from the query, never sent as `18?8`.
    39	- **Rationale**: One call per stone keeps SerpApi quota spend predictable. Obituary and grave index pages both carry name + dates, which is what identity matching needs.
    40	- **Rejected**:
    41	  - Multiple engines or providers: PRD Stretch.
    42	  - A Find a Grave scraper: no API and terms restrict it. SerpApi results that link there are fine.
    43	- **Interface**: `SearchProvider.search(query): Promise<SourceRecord[]>`, with one implementation (`serpapi.ts`).
    44	
    45	## R6. Gated and paywalled sources
    46	
    47	- **Decision**: A static deny-list of hostnames is applied to search results before identity matching: `ancestry.*`, `newspapers.com`, `genealogybank.com`, `myheritage.*`, `findmypast.*`, `newspaperarchive.com`, `fold3.com`. A page fetch that returns 401/402/403 or a login redirect drops that source.
    48	- **Rationale**: PRD §6 excludes paywalled and login-gated sources. A static list covers the big genealogy paywalls, and the fetch check catches the rest.
    49	- **Rejected**: Detecting paywalls by page content, which is too fuzzy for a deterministic rule.
    50	
    51	## R7. Identity resolution
    52	
    53	- **Decision**:
    54	  1. The model groups search results into candidate people with a structured output: `{ name, born, died, place, resultIds[] }`.
    55	  2. Code then:
    56	     - drops unknown `resultIds`;
    57	     - drops any result claimed by more than one candidate from all of them, which prevents silent merges;
    58	     - drops candidates whose known years conflict with the inscription (a `?` digit matches any digit);
    59	     - drops candidates left with no results;
    60	     - caps the list at 5, ordered by the number of matching inscription fields.
    61	  3. The visitor always confirms, even when only one candidate remains.
    62	- **Rationale**: Clustering free text into people is model work. Conflict and merge rules are deterministic and testable (Constitution III).
    63	- **Rejected**: Pure string scoring, which can't tell two "John Smith 1950–2011" obituaries apart by snippet alone.
    64	
    65	## R8. Story grounding (fetch page text)
    66	
    67	- **Decision**: After confirmation, the story pipeline:
    68	  1. Fetches the candidate's source pages in memory, at most 5 in parallel with an 8 s timeout and a 2 MB cap each.
    69	     - Honors robots.txt (`robots-parser`) for user agent `Gravespeaker`.
    70	     - Extracts the main text with `@mozilla/readability` on a `linkedom` DOM.
    71	     - Falls back to the search snippet when a fetch fails.
    72	  2. Sends the extracted text to the story agent, which returns sentences: `{ text, kind: 'fact' | 'reconstruction', claim: 'name' | 'birth' | 'death' | 'other', sourceIds[], quote }`.
    73	  3. Code keeps a `fact` sentence only if every `sourceId` belongs to the candidate and its `quote` appears, after normalization, in one cited source's text. Otherwise the sentence is dropped.
    74	  4. If no surviving fact has `claim: 'other'` with a quote containing a token beyond the deceased's name, month names and digits, the response is `insufficient` (spec FR-013). The model's `claim` label alone is never trusted for the bar.
    75	  5. Fetched text is never returned to the browser or stored.
    76	- **Rationale**: The user chose page text over snippets (2026-10-27). Snippets alone would fail the evidence bar on most stones. Quote matching gives a deterministic check against fabrication. The quote is never displayed, so source content isn't republished.
    77	- **Relatives** (user decision, 2026-10-27): relationships are allowed as cited facts ("my wife of 52 years"). A relative may be named only when a cited source says they died first ("preceded in death by"). Survivors are never named. The story agent's instructions enforce this, and the grounding benchmark (next spec) measures it with obituaries that list survivors. No code check: telling a survivor's name from a predeceased relative's takes reading comprehension, not a pattern.
    78	- **Rejected**: Snippets only (user rejected); `jsdom`, which is heavier than `linkedom`; a headless browser, which is far too heavy.

    82	- **Decision**: The story endpoint receives source URLs from the client, so `fetchPage` checks every request:

## R8. Story grounding (fetch page text)

- **Decision**: After confirmation, the story pipeline:
  1. Fetches the candidate's source pages in memory, at most 5 in parallel with an 8 s timeout and a 2 MB cap each.
     - Honors robots.txt (`robots-parser`) for user agent `Gravespeaker`.
     - Extracts the main text with `@mozilla/readability` on a `linkedom` DOM.
     - Falls back to the search snippet when a fetch fails.
  2. Sends the extracted text to the story agent, which returns sentences: `{ text, kind: 'fact' | 'reconstruction', claim: 'name' | 'birth' | 'death' | 'other', sourceIds[], quote }`.
  3. Code keeps a `fact` sentence only if every `sourceId` belongs to the candidate and its `quote` appears, after normalization, in one cited source's text. Otherwise the sentence is dropped.
  4. If no surviving fact has `claim: 'other'` with a quote containing a token beyond the deceased's name, month names and digits, the response is `insufficient` (spec FR-013). The model's `claim` label alone is never trusted for the bar.
  5. Fetched text is never returned to the browser or stored.
- **Rationale**: The user chose page text over snippets (2026-10-27). Snippets alone would fail the evidence bar on most stones. Quote matching gives a deterministic check against fabrication. The quote is never displayed, so source content isn't republished.
- **Relatives** (user decision, 2026-10-27): relationships are allowed as cited facts ("my wife of 52 years"). A relative may be named only when a cited source says they died first ("preceded in death by"). Survivors are never named. The story agent's instructions enforce this, and the grounding benchmark (next spec) measures it with obituaries that list survivors. No code check: telling a survivor's name from a predeceased relative's takes reading comprehension, not a pattern.
- **Rejected**: Snippets only (user rejected); `jsdom`, which is heavier than `linkedom`; a headless browser, which is far too heavy.

## R9. SSRF on page fetch

- **Decision**: The story endpoint receives source URLs from the client, so `fetchPage` checks every request:
  - only `https:`/`http:` URLs;
  - resolves DNS and rejects loopback, private, link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, which includes the metadata server), CGNAT and ULA addresses;
  - follows redirects manually, at most 3 hops, re-checking each hop.
- **Rationale**: On Cloud Run, an open fetch can reach the metadata server and leak the service account token. Signing candidates server-side would need a new secret, and CLAUDE.md requires asking before adding one.
- **Rejected**: HMAC-signed candidate payloads, which need a new Secret Manager secret; re-running search in the story request, which doubles SerpApi spend.

## R10. Upload limits and formats

## R8. Story grounding (fetch page text)

- **Decision**: After confirmation, the story pipeline:
  1. Fetches the candidate's source pages in memory, at most 5 in parallel with an 8 s timeout and a 2 MB cap each.
     - Honors robots.txt (`robots-parser`) for user agent `Gravespeaker`.
     - Extracts the main text with `@mozilla/readability` on a `linkedom` DOM.
     - Falls back to the search snippet when a fetch fails.
  2. Sends the extracted text to the story agent, which returns sentences: `{ text, kind: 'fact' | 'reconstruction', claim: 'name' | 'birth' | 'death' | 'other', sourceIds[], quote }`.
  3. Code keeps a `fact` sentence only if every `sourceId` belongs to the candidate and its `quote` appears, after normalization, in one cited source's text. Otherwise the sentence is dropped.
  4. If no surviving fact has `claim: 'other'` with a quote containing a token beyond the deceased's name, month names and digits, the response is `insufficient` (spec FR-013). The model's `claim` label alone is never trusted for the bar.
  5. Fetched text is never returned to the browser or stored.
- **Rationale**: The user chose page text over snippets (2026-10-27). Snippets alone would fail the evidence bar on most stones. Quote matching gives a deterministic check against fabrication. The quote is never displayed, so source content isn't republished.
- **Relatives** (user decision, 2026-10-27): relationships are allowed as cited facts ("my wife of 52 years"). A relative may be named only when a cited source says they died first ("preceded in death by"). Survivors are never named. The story agent's instructions enforce this, and the grounding benchmark (next spec) measures it with obituaries that list survivors. No code check: telling a survivor's name from a predeceased relative's takes reading comprehension, not a pattern.
- **Rejected**: Snippets only (user rejected); `jsdom`, which is heavier than `linkedom`; a headless browser, which is far too heavy.

## R9. SSRF on page fetch

- **Decision**: The story endpoint receives source URLs from the client, so `fetchPage` checks every request:
  - only `https:`/`http:` URLs;
  - resolves DNS and rejects loopback, private, link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, which includes the metadata server), CGNAT and ULA addresses;
  - follows redirects manually, at most 3 hops, re-checking each hop.
- **Rationale**: On Cloud Run, an open fetch can reach the metadata server and leak the service account token. Signing candidates server-side would need a new secret, and CLAUDE.md requires asking before adding one.
- **Rejected**: HMAC-signed candidate payloads, which need a new Secret Manager secret; re-running search in the story request, which doubles SerpApi spend.
